A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same utility-learning and steering research. All 23 pages of v1 and 18 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable; equations, algorithms, and the constructed game example support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports algorithms, mathematical bounds, proofs, and a constructed game counterexample. No original experimental, simulation, user-study, or data-analysis results appear in the main text or appendices.

after.justification: v2 remains theoretical throughout Sections 4–5 and Appendices A–D. It reports no original experimental, simulation, user-study, or data-analysis results.

M1.justification: v2 removes the rationalizable-agent learning algorithms and single-rational-agent payment-minimizing algorithm (v1 Algorithms 1, 2, and 5). The retained no-regret algorithms update using observed mixed strategies instead of sampled one-hot actions, while allowing sampled actions as a special case. Steering now computes an optimal exact CEP of the estimated game, replacing v1 Algorithm 6's optimal 2-epsilon-CEP.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or conducts training or evaluation. Changes to the behavioral models concern theoretical scope, not experimentally tested dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version reports evaluated empirical comparators. Binary search, gradient descent, and other no-regret algorithms are discussed analytically rather than compared through experiments.

E3.justification: Neither version contains experimental evaluation protocols, splits, metrics, or budgets. Changes to observations and algorithm horizons concern the theoretical procedures and assumptions.

E4.justification: Neither version reports empirical ablations, robustness tests, or error analyses. The matching-pennies counterexample is retained from v1 Proposition 7.4 to v2 Proposition D.5; its rewritten proof is a theoretical revision.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental runs, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Changes to probabilistic regret guarantees and concentration arguments are theoretical changes rather than empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Neither version reports measured performance results. The illustrative matching-pennies payoffs and principal objective value of -1/3 are unchanged. Revisions to analytical complexity guarantees are assessed under T1.

T1.justification: v2 removes the rationalizable-model upper bounds and single-rational-agent payment guarantee. Appendix C.1 revises the multi-agent error derivation and states explicit polynomial bounds; Appendix C.2 changes the regret lower-bound term from C^2/epsilon^2 to C^2/(4epsilon^2). Appendix D generalizes noncanonical CEPs and replaces v1's Nash-equilibrium-based steering upper-bound proof with a contextual swap-regret argument for uncoupled agents. The steering derivation also changes. These are substantive revisions beyond relocating proofs.

C1.justification: v1 presents learning under two behavioral models, their strict complexity separation, and the single-agent bounded-payment result as contributions. v2 removes those rationalizable-model contributions and focuses its abstract, introduction, and conclusion on arbitrary no-regret agents. Polynomial utility learning and optimal steering without known utilities remain central claims.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly discusses agents initially lacking knowledge of their own utilities and explains sampled-action observations as an extension of its mixed-strategy formulation. Section 6 adds learning through payments without signals as an open question. The negative-regret mechanism explanation and normal-form applicability limitation remain.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix C.1 provides explicit polynomial choices for the learning-phase length and total rounds where v1 left the final dependence as poly(M). Steering configuration guidance changes from L=T^(3/4) to L=T^(2/3), retaining rho=T^(-1/4). Neither version supplies experimental implementation artifacts or code-access information.

R1.justification: Section 1.2 substantially expands and revises research positioning. Added works include Peng et al. (2019), Canyakmaz et al. (2024), Zhang et al. (2025), and Alanqary et al. (2026). v2 explicitly contrasts payments-enabled learning with impossibility results for learning in Stackelberg settings and broadens the steering and opponent-learning discussion. Rationalizability references disappear with that research branch.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution overview, related work, and model exposition are extensively rewritten around no-regret learning. Payment complexity moves to Appendix A, and much of the learning and CEP analysis moves into expanded appendices. The contents page disappears, preliminaries are consolidated, and author affiliations are updated.

P2.justification: v2 comprehensively adopts the ICLR layout, with a redesigned author block, conference headers, and an opening page combining the abstract and introduction. Algorithm displays are removed or reformatted, and the retained payoff matrix and CEP linear program move into Appendix D. This changes the document's visual organization throughout.

improvement.justification: v2 offers a clearer no-regret focus and more explicit derivations, but introduces mathematical statement–proof discrepancies. Theorem 4.4 states Omega(nM log(1/epsilon)), while Appendix C.2 still derives a bound divided by log M. Theorem 5.2 states o(T^(-1/2)), while Appendix D.3 supplies only O(T^(-1/2)); v1's corresponding statements retain the logarithmic qualification and O-rate. These unresolved discrepancies make the net quality effect of the clearer presentation and revised theoretical arguments uncertain.
